activities.anchor: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples
activities.caption: pair each learning family with its fuel
activities.name: mlFamiliesMatch

config.prompt: Pair each learning family with what it learns from:

pairs.right: labelled examples — classification for categories, regression for numbers

config.why: The inversion that defines the field: behaviour learned from examples rather than specified by a programmer.

activities.anchor: A classifier eats a feature vector x
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the classifier's anatomy
activities.name: mlClassifierCloze

config.text: A classifier eats a %%0%% vector and outputs a predicted label, usually via %%1%% per class that are turned into probabilities. Logistic regression's decision boundary is a %%2%% surface through feature space; neural networks stack learned transformations until the boundary can take almost any shape.
config.hint: What goes in, what comes out before the threshold, and the shape of the line logistic regression draws.

activities.anchor: it will happily use a feature that is a symptom rather
activities.caption: the leadership question the model cannot answer
activities.name: mlCausalBranch

config.root: Your churn model leans hard on 'past support tickets'. Leadership asks: if we reduce support tickets, will churn fall?

choices.label: Probably — the model shows tickets drive churn
choices.feedback: The model is a machine for conditional correlation: tickets may be a symptom of dissatisfaction, not its cause — intervening on a symptom can accomplish nothing.

choices.label: Not from this model — causal claims need experimental design
choices.feedback: Randomise an intervention on a subset of customers and measure — the A/B lesson's randomisation is what turns prediction into causal knowledge.

choices.label: Retrain with more features until the cause appears
choices.feedback: More features add correlation, not causation — the confounders just get better company.

symptom.text: Past support tickets predict churn; they do not cause it. The model's accuracy says nothing about what intervention would work.

design.text: However accurate the predictions, prediction alone never supplies cause — design does.

more.text: The model now predicts even better and still cannot say what happens if you act.

config.why: A trained model is a machine for conditional correlation — causal claims need experimental design, however accurate the predictions.

activities.anchor: The train/test split is the field's founding ritual
activities.caption: rebuild the working loop in order
activities.name: mlLoopOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the working loop — what comes first:
items: Split — hold out 20% the model never sees
Baseline — write down the dumbest reasonable competitor's score
Fit — the simplest thing that could work
Diagnose — plot training and validation errors side by side
Regularise — penalise complexity until the gap closes
config.why: An order of operations, not a buffet: the split comes first because every later number is worthless without it, and the baseline second because a model only means something relative to the cheapest alternative.

activities.caption: which curve is the honest grade?
activities.name: mlCurveTrace

config.prompt: Two error curves as model capacity grows — which one is validation error?
config.why: Curve B is validation error: it falls as capacity captures real structure, then rises as capacity starts fitting noise — the U of the bias–variance dial, and the gap between the curves is the overfitting.

activities.anchor: The remedies, in the order practitioners reach for them
activities.caption: file each remedy under the lever it pulls
activities.name: mlRemedySort

config.prompt: File each remedy under the lever it pulls:

items.label: noise averages out while signal persists
L1 drives uninformative weights to exactly zero
early stopping halts at the validation minimum

config.why: The same lever with different handles — and more data is the only one that never hurts, because it changes what the model sees rather than how flexible it is.

activities.caption: two models on Tuesday — drag the divider
activities.name: mlGapCompare

config.prompt: Two models, same dataset — drag the divider:

before.label: 99% train / 71% test
before.text: a memoriser — brilliant on questions it has seen, worse than the baseline when real customers arrive

after.label: 85% train / 84% test
after.text: a learner — a modest gap, patterns that transfer

config.why: Training accuracy is nearly free; the informative number is test performance relative to training performance — the gap is the overfitting.

activities.anchor: Suppose a missed fraud costs 500 dollars
activities.caption: call the current threshold's bill
activities.name: mlCostEst

config.prompt: A missed fraud costs $500, each review costs $5. The model misses 20 frauds and triggers 200 reviews. What is the total bill?
config.why: 20 × 500 + 200 × 5 = $11,000 — and lowering the threshold to catch 90 (flagging 500) cuts the bill to $7,500 for these costs. There is no best threshold in the abstract, only the best for a stated price list.
config.context: at $50 per review the verdict flips — the metric conversation is a business conversation

activities.anchor: the default winners on tabular business data
activities.caption: pair each model family with its honest territory
activities.name: mlDomainMatch

config.prompt: Pair each model family with the territory where it wins:

pairs.right: transparent, fast, surprisingly hard to beat on tabular data — always try first
the default winners on tabular business data, with little tuning
dominant on images, audio and text — data-hungry and opaque
the unsupervised default for segmentation — clusters are judgement calls, not outputs

config.why: The differences are in flexibility, assumptions and cost — not in goal: every family estimates the same object, the probability of the class given the features.
